t: I heard the child breathe before I realised I had been holding my own breath.
The mother looked exhausted, but she smiled when they placed the child beside her.
I waited outside until someone opened the door and said both were safe.
The healer asked for water, cloth, and quiet. Prayer came from everyone else.
I saw how close it came. Luck feels like too small a word.
The child did not cry at once. I prayed before deciding whether I believed.
When the child finally moved, everyone thanked somebody different.
I watched the healer stay calm while the rest of us failed at it.
The mother asked us to stop whispering and let her work.
I thought we had lost the child. Then I heard a cry.
Someone prayed beside me. I joined before I could question myself.
The room was all work until the child arrived. Then everybody started thanking the god.
I saw skill, strength, and something I still cannot name.
The birth lasted through the night. Dawn found both of them alive.
I brought clean water and tried not to listen through the door.
The healer said the danger had passed. I nearly thanked the god aloud.
I watched the mother hold the child and forgot every doubt for a moment.
Nothing looked miraculous until I remembered how frightened we had been.
The child was small, loud, and alive. I needed nothing more just then.
I saw the mother's hands stop shaking when the child cried.
We did everything we knew. Perhaps the part beyond knowing mattered too.
The room smelled of smoke and blood. Nobody there spoke lightly of miracles.
I stood useless by the wall and promised anything if both survived.
Both lived. I am still deciding what to do with the promise I made.
The child gripped one finger. That felt important, though I cannot explain why.
I expected a sign and got a tired mother asking for water.
People called the birth blessed. I called it a relief and meant nearly the same thing.
The healer never mentioned the god. Everyone waiting outside did.
I prayed for both lives, then spent the whole birth doubting my own prayer.
The first cry sounded ordinary. I have never been happier to hear something ordinary.
That sounds like help, but it also sounds like very good healing.
I am glad they are safe. I can wonder about the reason later.
Did the mother think the god helped, or is that everyone else's account?
A safe birth can feel divine without proving anything.
I would rather thank too many hands than overlook one.
Maybe the god answered. Maybe the healer did. I can honour both.
Was the child ever in danger, or did it only feel that way?
I want to believe your prayer mattered. I truly do.
Good news makes belief easier, but easy belief still worries me.
The mother deserves rest before we turn her birth into doctrine.
I cannot call it chance after hearing how close they came.
Perhaps mercy and skill arrived together. Why must we choose?
Did anyone ask the healer what happened?
I prayed for them too. I was afraid to tell anybody.
The child's survival matters more than settling this argument.
That account leaves room for the god, though it does not require one.
I believe you saw something good. I am unsure what made it happen.
Maybe answered prayers look exactly like people doing their work well.
I hope the god helped. Hope is the honest word.
Your story makes me grateful and uncertain in equal measure.
Was anyone listening when the mother spoke afterwards?
The god may deserve thanks, but the healer certainly does.
I have heard enough bad birth stories to value this one.
One safe child cannot settle every doubt, but it can quiet them.
That sounds wonderful. It also sounds exhausting.
I am not ready to name it a miracle. I am ready to celebrate.
Let us ask what the family needs instead of what the birth proves.
I should visit them before deciding what I believe about it.
We can debate the god after the mother has slept.
I will bring clean cloth. That is one thing I know how to do.
The story gives me questions. The family needs useful hands.
I may pray tonight. I will decide when I am alone.
Let the child become a person before we make them an argument.
I need to hear the healer's account before settling mine.
That is good news, whatever name we give the cause.
I will think about the god after checking on the mother.
Perhaps I owe thanks. I know I owe the family some peace.
We should stop before we turn uncertainty into gossip.
I am relieved enough for today. Belief can wait until tomorrow.
The child is safe. I do not need a second conclusion yet.
I should bring supper and keep my questions to myself.
Tell me again after the excitement has left the account.
I believe the relief in your face. The rest needs time.
Maybe we were helped. We were certainly fortunate.
I will not argue about miracles beside a sleeping child.
There is joy enough here without forcing certainty onto it.
The family will need food tomorrow. Let us start there.
I should stop talking about them and go see how they are.
A new child means more work for everyone. Good work, though.
Let us give them one quiet evening before visiting.
I will pass the good news on and leave out the argument.
The child has arrived. The village can meet them soon enough.
I need to finish my work before offering anybody help.
We should remember the healer when thanking people.
That family has heard enough voices for one day.
I am glad you told me. I will let the news settle.
Do you know whether the mother had asked for the god?
Was the healer surprised, or only everyone watching?
I wonder what the mother believes happened in that room.
The first cry must have changed every thought you had.
Did your prayer feel answered, or were you simply relieved?
I might believe differently if I had stood where you stood.
People outside the room always sound more certain than people inside it.
Perhaps the god worked through the healer. I could accept that.
Was there a moment when everyone thought the child was lost?
I keep wondering whether blessings always look like ordinary work.
Your uncertainty makes the account easier for me to trust.
I expected you to sound more certain after seeing it.
Maybe nobody in that room needs to agree about why they survived.
The god may have helped, but the mother still bore the pain.
I understand why that birth changed something in you.
